title: Helen Humes and why some singers are left out of books
summary: Helen Humes sang and recorded his song; he says publicity at the right time explains who makes the books.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: And doing the blues (inaudible) back in Chicago many, many years ago, 19 -- I don't know what li, 19 something.
And I think she was at the Freeman. I'm not sure. I was out -- I have to be out of here. It's very difficult for me to --
Oh, you're okay. No, listen. First, we're going back so many years. Do you -- now, you wrote for Helen Hume, didn't you?
I didn't write for her. She sang for me.
Yeah, I recorded her, Helen Humes.
She sang my song. I taught her my song and recorded her.
Which -- do you recall which song that was?
I can't remember that, but I have a record of it.
Sure. Sure. All right. Now, why -- we

looked in the books. I mean I've talked to you about going through 20, 30 books, and there is so little reference, maybe a word here on Helen Humes. Now, yet somebody like Alberta Hunter really made the Book on Jazz. And Helen Humes was omitted. Now, what do you think -- how does something like that happen?
Well, that's ordinary. Some people get more publicity than that -- they get the right publicity at the right time and the right place (inaudible). But that's easy to understand.
